issues.legal_issue: A criminal investigation must seek the complete and unvarnished truth rather than merely assemble evidence supporting the prosecution.
material_facts: The prosecution described a single incident, but the record contained evidence of injuries to members of both sides and indications of a dispute and possible events at another field.
The investigating officer knew that members of the accused side had injuries but did not ask witnesses how those injuries had occurred.

The investigating officer did not fully investigate signs of trampling and ploughing or other circumstances relevant to the competing account, and important injuries and events were omitted from the report and witness statements.
issues.conclusion: The investigating officer's duty was to bring out the real, unvarnished truth, not merely to bolster the prosecution case; the investigation in this case did not sufficiently examine relevant facts.
issues.legal_principle: An investigating officer must investigate impartially and seek the real, unvarnished truth, including facts that may support the defence. Where neither side presents the whole account, a court may draw limited inferences from proved facts and circumstances to assess whether reasonable doubt exists. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this principle in the supplied judgment.

predicates.criminal_case_under_investigation: A criminal case was being investigated by an investigating officer.
predicates.material_evidence_supports_competing_acc: Evidence or circumstances in the case supported materially different accounts of how the occurrence happened.
predicates.injuries_on_both_sides: People on both sides of the alleged encounter had injuries.
predicates.investigating_officer_failed_to_examine_: The investigating officer did not adequately inquire into relevant evidence or circumstances that could support the defence account.

issues.definition: When a criminal investigation has material competing evidence or injuries on both sides and the investigating officer fails to examine relevant defence evidence, the officer must seek the complete truth.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for a fatal injury cannot stand where the evidence leaves reasonable doubt that the accused caused that injury.
material_facts: Only three witnesses attributed the fatal blow to the accused, while many other witnesses with an equally good opportunity to observe did not implicate him or mention the attack on the deceased.
The accounts did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that the fatal injury was caused by the accused rather than another person, and the circumstances of the injury remained uncertain.
issues.conclusion: The accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt on the fatal injury and was acquitted of the offence under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove the accused's responsibility for the fatal injury beyond reasonable doubt. Material omissions by witnesses who had an equally good opportunity to observe, together with uncertainty about who inflicted the injury, may create reasonable doubt. The Court applied the benefit-of-doubt principle to the charge under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code; no earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The matter is a criminal appeal against a conviction.
predicates.fatal_injury_attributed_to_accused: The prosecution alleged that the accused caused an injury that resulted in death.
predicates.equally_well_placed_witnesses_do_not_imp: Witnesses with an equally good opportunity to observe did not implicate the accused in causing the fatal injury.
predicates.evidence_leaves_identity_of_assailant_un: The evidence does not establish beyond reasonable doubt who caused the fatal injury.

issues.definition: In an appeal against conviction for a fatal injury, when the evidence leaves the assailant's identity uncertain, including because equally well-placed witnesses do not implicate the accused, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt on the fatal charge.

issues.legal_issue: Specific testimony from injured witnesses can support convictions for the assaults they describe, and group-offence convictions may be sustained where the evidence justifies applying the rules of unlawful assembly liability.
material_facts: Several witnesses had themselves been injured and gave specific accounts identifying the accused who struck them.
The Court found no shown motive for an injured witness to substitute a wrong person for the actual assailant.
The evidence supported the application of Sections 147 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code to the accused whose convictions were before the Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the convictions supported by the injured witnesses' specific accounts and held that applying Sections 147 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code to the accused was justified.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered an injured witness reliable as to the identity of the person who inflicted that witness's injuries, particularly where no motive to falsely substitute an assailant was shown. It held that Sections 147 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code were properly applied on the evidence in this case. No earlier case is cited in the supplied judgment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_convictions and injured_witness_identifies_specific_assailant and no_shown_motive_to_substitute_assailant and evidence_supports_group_offence_liability

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_convictions: The matter is a criminal appeal challenging convictions.
predicates.injured_witness_identifies_specific_assa: A witness injured in the occurrence specifically identified the person who inflicted that witness's injury.
predicates.no_shown_motive_to_substitute_assailant: The evidence did not show a motive for the injured witness to identify someone other than the actual assailant.
predicates.evidence_supports_group_offence_liabilit: The evidence supported the accused's participation in a group whose conduct permitted group-offence liability to be applied.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, specific identification by an injured witness without a shown motive to substitute an assailant, together with evidence supporting group-offence liability, may sustain the specific-assault and group-offence convictions.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal appellate court may reduce sentences to the periods already served when the convictions are maintained and the appellants have served almost all of their sentences.
material_facts: The Court maintained the convictions of the appellants, except that one appellant was acquitted of the fatal-injury charge while remaining convicted of a group offence.
The Court was informed that each convicted appellant had served almost the whole period of the sentence imposed.
issues.conclusion: The Court reduced the appellants' sentences to the periods already undergone and directed their release unless they were wanted in another matter.
issues.legal_principle: In disposing of a criminal appeal, the Court may modify the sentence while maintaining a conviction, taking account of the period already served and the interests of justice. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this sentencing decision in the supplied judgment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_sentence: The matter is a criminal appeal that puts the sentence before the court for consideration.
predicates.conviction_is_maintained: The court maintains the relevant conviction on appeal.
predicates.sentence_almost_fully_served: The person convicted has served almost all of the sentence imposed.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal concerns sentence, the conviction is maintained, and almost all of the sentence has been served, the sentence is reduced to the period already served.
